messages.subject: INTEGER PARAMETER, hierarchical model
parts:
Hi Stan,

I'm converting from Jags to Stan and this is one of my first Stan-programs.
I read from previous discussions about the declaration problems of integer parameters.
I read the manual, in particular the chapter of finite mixtures, as suggested in plenty of previous posts.

The model I mean to compute is a hierarchical one(logit regression), with hierarchical priors.
I'm running this model from R and I bumped into the error message at bottom.
How may I face with this problem and how may I solve it?

data{
        int<lower=0> N;
        int<lower=0> k; // number of predictors
        matrix[N,k] x;
        int <lower=0,upper=1> y[N]; // y is a binary variable
        real<lower=0> sd1;
        real<lower=0> sd2;
}

parameters{
            vector[k] betak;
            real<lower=0,upper=1> hk[k];  // i'd like hk to be an integer but i           
                                                           cannot, according to Stan
            real<lower=0>sdk[k];
            real<lower=0,upper=1>pk[k];
}

model{
     for( j in 1:k){
         pk[j] ~ beta(1,1);
         hk[j]~ bernoulli(pk[j]);
          sdk[j] <- (1-hk[j])*sd1 + (1+hk[j])*sd2;
          betak[j] ~ normal(0,sdk[j]);
                }
        for(n in 1:N)
                y[n]~bernoulli_logit((beta[n]))
}

I think the problem is the discrete support of bernoulli distribution, which is in contrast with the declaration of the parameter hk.
(The vectorization of this code is my future goal)
Thanks a lot,
Luke

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] INTEGER PARAMETER, hierarchical model
parts:
Your diagnosis of the problem is correct --- the outcome of a Bernoulli
must be discrete, but Stan doesn't support integer parameters.

There's a new chapter in the manual on marginalizing out integer parameters,
which is a bit more general than the mixtures chapter and goes into more coding
detail.

> for( j in 1:k){
> pk[j] ~ beta(1,1);
> hk[j]~ bernoulli(pk[j]);
> sdk[j] <- (1-hk[j])*sd1 + (1+hk[j])*sd2;
> betak[j] ~ normal(0,sdk[j]);
> }
> for(n in 1:N)
> y[n]~bernoulli_logit((beta[n]))
> }
First off, formatting always helps with debugging:

> for (j in 1:k) {
> pk[j] ~ beta(1,1);
> hk[j] ~ bernoulli(pk[j]);
> sdk[j] <- (1-hk[j])*sd1 + (1+hk[j])*sd2;
> betak[j] ~ normal(0,sdk[j]);
> }
> for (n in 1:N)
> y[n] ~ bernoulli_logit((beta[n]))

I'm confused because beta isn't defined anywhere and if it's
supposed to be the same as betak, then betak is indexed 1:k
and beta 1:N. I also don't get the 1-hk and 1+hk for a bernoulli,
the first of which will take on values in 0:1 and the second in 1:2.

- Bob

I read chapter 6 of the manual(my manuale is the one updated on 20th October 2014) about marginalization.
I'd like to ask some  questions about general implementation since I read different posts with problems of implementation and I think that my model is a very general hierarchical one.

My idea is to marginalized in the following sense, with the goal of computing the log posterior density log(betak|y)
log p(betak|y)= SUM_n{ p(betak | hk,pk,y) * p(hk |pk,y)* p( pk| y)}
so as to deal with uniform_log(y,0,1)+bernoulli_log(). Do you agree with this marginalization?

My first question is: how may I include in bernoulli_log's parameters function when l'm interested (for Bernoulli) in the parameter sampled at the previous step by the uniform distribution? May you give me any suggestions for dealing with the marginalization in a loop?

Then, if I assigned a normal distribution for the intercept beta0 ( for example ~ normal(0,0.01) ), may you think that the following Stan-statements are correct and optimal?

for(i in 1:N){
       for(j in 1:k){
         tp[i,j]<- betak[j]*x[i,j];
                    };
            mu[i]<- beta0+cumulative_sum(tp[i,]));            
                }
 with mu a vector[k] parameter and tmp an auxiliary parameter( matrix[N,k]).
In this case, y must be sampled from  bernoulli_logit(mu[n]), re-coding the loop as
for( n in 1:N){
     y[n]~ bernoulli_logit(mu[n]);
}
Where may I include the introduction of beta0, since this final sampling depends on betak and beta0, and, implicitly, on hk?

Finally, just a question for curiosity: l looked in the manual, but l didn't find any stan functions for Bernoulli(Phi) ( but I found bernoulli_logit_log); is there no implementation for it?

parts:
Hi!
I studied the chapter about latent discrete parameters and I found it very interesting and effective,summarizing different cases, that, thanks to this chapter, may be translated from BUGS/JAGS to Stan easily.
This chapter clarify me different things about marginalization: I'm new at Stan and I rarely do marginalization.
However, I wish you could help me clarifying some implementation steps.
I remind my model is the following one:
I have N observations and I would like to do logit regression on them, following a hierarchical model:

hk~ Bernoulli(0.5)
betak | hk  ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) )

Thus: Y| betak,hk  ~ bernoulli_logit ( beta0+ betak* x)

 My original code is this and then i reported my corrections:

data{
        int<lower=0> N;
        int<lower=0> k; // number of predictors
matrix[N,k] x;     // matrix of predictors

int <lower=0,upper=1> y[N]; // y is a binary variable
        real<lower=0> sd1;
        real<lower=0> sd2;
}

parameters{
            vector[k] betak;
            real<lower=0,upper=1> hk[k];  // i'd like hk to be an integer but i           
                                                           cannot, according to Stan

vector[N] beta0;
           
}

model{

     beta0 ~ normal(0,0.00001);
for( j in 1:k){

hk[j]~ bernoulli(0.5);   // here, it's the big problem
       
            betak[j] ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) );
                      }
        for(n in 1:N)
                y[n]~bernoulli_logit((beta0+ betak* x[n]))

}

After your suggestions about marginalization, I tried to consider  hk as a latent discrete parameter and draw the log likelihood:

p( y | betak ) = SUM_{0,1} P(y| betak,hk)* P( hk l betak )
             =SUM_{0,1} Bernoulli(hk l 0.5) * PROD (Bernoulli_logit(beta0+betak* x ))

Then I computed the log likelihood:
logp(yl betak) =log_sum_exp( Bernoulli( hk l 0.5) )+
                        SUM_(n in 1:N) Bernoulli_logit(beta0+betak* x )

In this marginalization I don't take into account the fact that betak ~ normal(0,(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) ) so my great doubt is: since, in order to compute the likelihood, I have to know about betak, how do I have to introduce this fact?

Maybe I'm wrong, but I think it's the crucial point for implementation.
Start by saying that I'm new at Stan functions like log_sum_exp and increment_log_prob I think to solve this problems, working in the transformed parameters block and acting on the likelihood in the model block (using increment_log_prob of log posterior.
May you give me any suggestions for the implementation?
I talk over this topic(the implementation) with one of my colleagues who uses BUGS but our discussion turned out to be disastrous: I would like to use Stan from now on and I'm trying to convince him to use it.
Thanks a lot,
Luke

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] INTEGER PARAMETER, hierarchical model
parts:
It's easier to convince people with a working example.
In our experience, marginalizing out discrete parameters leads
to models that fit on the order of 100 to 1000 times faster
than the BUGS/JAGS versions that sample the discrete parameters,
and also have much better robustness and tail behavior.

Having said that, I don't think you can marginalize
in a computationally tractable way in your problem.

You write this

> hk~ Bernoulli(0.5)
> betak | hk ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) )

but then translate as:

> beta0 ~ normal(0,0.00001);

Stan uses std-dev as the parameter for normal, not precision,
so this is probably the wrong scale for your problem. I'd recommend
tighter priors --- there are sections in the manual on recommended
priors in the regression chapter.

But the real problem is here:

> for( j in 1:k){
>
> hk[j]~ bernoulli(0.5); // here, it's the big problem
>
> betak[j] ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) );
> }
> for(n in 1:N)
> y[n]~bernoulli_logit((beta0+ betak* x[n]))
>

I'm assuming you meant x[n] * betak (row vector * vector),
which produces a scalar. First, write out the joint
density including the discrete parameter:

p(hk,betak,y)
= PROD_j ( bernoulli(hk[j] | 0.5)
* normal(betak[j] | hk[j]*sd2 + (1-hk)* sd1) )
* PROD_n bernoulli_logit(y[n] | beta0 + x[n] * betak)

And then write out the margianlization:

p(betak,y) = SUM_hk p(hk) * p(betak,y|hk)

where the sum is over all 2^k configurations of hk. There's no
way to factor that 2^k down the way the examples are in the manual
because the likelihood isn't factored along with the marginalization.

What you want is something that looks like this:

SUM_{j in 1:k} SUM_{hk[j] in 0:1} p(hk[j]) * p(...|hk[j])

The only way your problem will work in Stan is if 2^k is not too large (on
the order of tens or hundreds rather than thousands or millions).
Then you can do the explicit summation, though it's not going to be pretty
code-wise.

- Bob
